analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators set safety standards for guns and ammunition and order recalls of defective firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 1997 with three House Democratic sponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then its Crime Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated guns and ammunition like other consumer products: the Treasury Department, through the ATF, could set safety standards for how firearms are designed and made, order recalls, repairs, or refunds for dangerous or defective guns, inspect factories and dealers, and fine violators. It would also let people harmed by violations sue for damages and would fund federal research into firearm deaths and injuries. It never moved past a House subcommittee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the public — including gun owners and people at risk of gun violence — would have gained federal safety standards for firearms, mandatory recalls of dangerous or defective products, a government clearinghouse publishing data on gun deaths and injuries, and the right to sue violators in court with attorney's fees available to winners. Consumers could compare the safety of different firearms, similar to how other consumer products are rated.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Directed the Treasury Secretary to issue safety regulations for the design, manufacture, and performance of firearms, parts, ammunition, and nonpowder (BB) guns to reduce 'unreasonable risk of injury' to the public.

Authorized orders requiring manufacturers and dealers to warn the public, repair, replace, recall, or refund the purchase price of firearm products found defective, out of compliance, or unreasonably risky.

Created a private right of action: anyone harmed by a violation could sue for damages, and any interested person could go to court to enforce the law, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs.

Required a federal Firearms Violence Information Clearinghouse, ongoing studies of firearm-related deaths and injuries, safety research, and annual public reporting — data collection the firearms industry does not face elsewhere.

Imposed civil fines for violations (starting at $5,000 per product, adjusted for inflation), court-ordered injunctions and seizures, and up to two years' imprisonment for knowingly violating the rules after notice.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, and pawnbrokers would bear the costs: testing and certifying products, new labeling and record-keeping, government inspections of their premises and records, fines for violations, and the cost of recalls, repairs, or refunds. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed on to gun buyers through higher prices. People and companies in the industry could also face civil suits from private plaintiffs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun and ammunition makers and dealers

drawbacks.text: The 'unreasonable risk of injury' standard gives an executive agency broad discretion over a constitutionally sensitive product; the Secretary could prohibit manufacture, import, or sale of an entire firearm product — not just fix defects — which opponents of gun regulation warned could extend beyond safety fixes to restricting firearms themselves.

The bill's private right of action and private enforcement suits, with attorney's fees, could generate substantial litigation costs for manufacturers and dealers, including small ones, on top of direct compliance costs.

The stockpiling provision made it unlawful to manufacture, purchase, or import a firearm product at a rate significantly above a pre-regulation base period between the time a rule is issued and when it takes effect — restricting otherwise lawful transactions during that window.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill applied a well-established model — consumer product safety regulation, like the system that covers toys, appliances, and cars — to the one major consumer product category that lacked it, and its core tools (safety standards, recalls, labeling, fines, and research) are ones most industries already operate under. The compliance and litigation costs to manufacturers and dealers are real, and the "unreasonable risk" standard does hand a single executive agency broad power over firearms design and availability, which is a fair objection given the product involved. On balance, the public-safety benefits — defect recalls, safety testing, and independent data on gun injuries — outweighed those costs, but the breadth of the agency's authority was a legitimate design concern the bill never had a chance to be refined through the normal committee process.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then its Crime Subcommittee in 1997 and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the Firearms Safety and Violence Prevention Act of 1997 on February 13, 1997, joined by Reps. Chuck Schumer and Alcee Hastings of Florida.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and on March 5, 1997 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor vote. The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and opponents of federal gun regulation are better off: guns remained the only major consumer product category with no federal safety regulation, no mandatory recalls of defective products, and no federal safety research mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun and ammunition makers and dealers

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; after the bill's referral to committee, the only action in the entire 105th Congress was a referral to a subcommittee one month later.

against.name: House Crime Subcommittee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after it was referred to the subcommittee on March 5, 1997; it sat there for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Long opposed consumer-product-safety regulation of firearms and supported keeping ATF's authority limited; the firearms lobby has consistently worked to keep such bills from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no voting pattern exists; the bill's only recorded support came from three House Democrats, and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected firearms and ammunition to the same kind of federal safety regulation, testing, certification, recall, and fine regime that applies to other consumer products, plus private lawsuits and inspections. The industry's interest in avoiding these rules ran directly against the bill's public-safety purpose.

Dealers and pawnbrokers, explicitly included in the definition of 'firearms dealer,' would have faced labeling requirements, new record-keeping obligations, inspections of their premises and records, civil fines for violations, and liability in private enforcement suits.
